en: May there be prosperity.
The Śrī Sītā Kavaca from within the Śrīmad Ānanda Rāmāyaṇa.
Agastya said:
"O child, you have asked well; listen with an attentive mind.
First, I shall describe the beautiful and auspicious armor (kavaca) of Sītā."
She who was born from the furrow for the sake of prosperity and reared by the protector of Mithilā;
she who became the daughter of King Padmākṣa and was won by Nala; she who emerged from a citron fruit;
she who merged into the jewel within the ocean; and she who entered the Veda as a syllable.
May that deer-eyed, moon-faced beloved of Rāma protect me in Laṅkā. || 2 ||
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Of this mantra, the Śrī Sītā-kavaca, Agastya is the seer (ṛṣi),
the venerable Sītā is the deity (devatā),
and Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ).
*Rameti* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Janakajā* is the power (*śakti*). *Vanije* is the pin (*kīlaka*). *Padmākṣasute* is the weapon (*astra*).
"Mātuliṅgī" is the armor (*kavaca*).
"Mūlakāsura-ghātinī" is the mantra.
[This is for] the sake of pleasing Śrī Sītārāmacandra; [it is] all...
The application is for the purpose of accomplishing one's desires during the recitation.
Now follows the placement of the fingers (aṅgulīnyāsa).
Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to Sītā with the two thumbs;
oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Ramā with the two index fingers;
oṃ hrūṃ, salutation to Janakajā with the two middle fingers.
Oṃ hraiṃ, salutation to Avanijā with the two ring fingers. Oṃ hrauṃ, salutation to Padmākṣasutā with the two little fingers.
Oṃ hraḥ, salutation to Mātuliṅgī with the palms and backs of the hands.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the heart and other [limbs].
Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Sītā, the heart; Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Ramā, the head;
Oṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to Janakajā, the tuft of hair.
Oṃ hraiṃ, for the armor of Avanijā, huṃ. Oṃ hrauṃ, for the three eyes of Padmākṣasutā, vauṣaṭ.
Oṃ hraḥ, for the weapon of Mātuliṅgī, phaṭ.
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om" is the binding of the directions.
Now, meditation.
Sītā, whose eyes are like lotus petals and whose radiance is equal to a mass of lightning—
two-armed, with delicate limbs, and clothed in yellow silk.
On the lion-throne, seated on the left side of Rāmacandra, was the excellent lady, adorned with various ornaments and wearing a pair of earrings. || 2 ||
Adorned with a crest-jewel, bracelets, armlets, a girdle, and anklets; with the sun and moon at her parting of the hair, and a tilaka mark upon her forehead.
Peacocks, adorned with ornaments, smelled the fragrant rays of her beauty;
[she was anointed with] turmeric, divine collyrium, saffron, and flowers.
She bore fragrant substances with excellent scent and luster; she had a smiling face and a fair complexion, and held a *mandāra* flower in her hand.
Holding in her other hand an unsurpassed citron,
she was clad in beautiful garments, possessed lips like the bimba fruit, and eyes like those of the moon-vehicled god.
He beheld the auspicious goddess Kalakaṇṭhā,
who was as beautiful as the moon, born from a citron fruit, and the daughter of Padmākṣa.
Thus meditating upon Maithilī, the beloved of Rāma, who was being fanned by female attendants, the daughter of Janaka, whose breasts were like golden jars; || 8 ||
The divine armor of Sītā, which brings about great welfare, should be recited.
Oṃ! May Śrī Sītā protect me from the east; may Jānakī protect me from the south;
may Vaidehī protect me from the west; and may Maithilī protect me from the north. (1)
May Mātuliṅgī protect me from below; may Padmākṣajā protect me from above;
may the daughter of the Wind-god protect me in the middle; and may Ramā protect me on all sides.
May the princess with her smiling face protect my head; may she protect my forehead;
may the lotus-eyed one protect the space between my eyebrows; and may the deer-eyed one protect my eyes. (3)
May the beloved of Śrī Rāma protect [my] cheek and the root of the ear;
may Sāttvikī protect the tip of the nose, and may Rājasī protect the face. 4.
May Tāmasī protect my speech; may the devoted wife protect my tongue; may Mahāmāyā protect my teeth; and may Kanakaprabhā protect my chin. (5)
May she of gentle form protect the throat; may she worshipped by the gods protect the shoulders;
may she of beautiful gait protect the arms; and may she adorned with bracelets protect the hands.
May she with the red nails protect my nails; may Laghūdarā protect my belly;
may the wife of Rāma protect my chest; and may she who deluded Rāvaṇa protect my sides. || 7 ||
May Vahniguptā always protect my back;
may Divyapradā protect the navel, and Rākṣasamohinī the hips.
May Ratnaguptā protect the secret parts; may Haripriyā protect the penis;
may Rambhoru protect the thighs; and may Priyabhāṣiṇī protect the knees.
May she of beautiful eyebrows always protect my shanks; may she who is fanned by chowries protect my ankles;
may the daughter of Lava protect my feet; and may Kuśāmbikā protect my limbs.
May she who has the tinkling of anklets always protect my toes;
may she who is clothed in yellow silk eternally guard my body hairs.
May she who takes the form of Time protect me at night, and she who is solely intent on giving at day;
may she, the slayer of the Asura Mūlaka, protect me at all times.
Thus, O Sutīkṣṇa, this armor of Sītā has been declared by me;
whoever, having risen in the morning and bathed, should recite this daily. (13)
Having worshipped Jānakī, one shall obtain all desires;
a seeker of wealth shall obtain riches, and a seeker of a son shall obtain a son.
One desiring a woman shall obtain an auspicious wife; one desiring happiness shall attain comfort.
One should always recite the armor (kavaca) of Sītā eight times.
A man should always devotedly offer eight types of fruits, flowers, and other items, such as those beginning with 'ka', individually to Sītā, the daughter of the Earth. (16)
Those men on earth who recite with devotion this meritorious armor of Sītā, which destroys all sins, are truly blessed. (17)
They recite the armor of Rāma without the armor of Sītā;
likewise, it is considered in vain without the armor of Lakṣmaṇa. (18)
Therefore, men should always recite the fourfold armor-mantras;
first that of the Son of the Wind, and after that, that of Lakṣmaṇa.
Then one should recite [the armor] of Sītā, and after that, that of Śrī Rāma;
thus this quartet of armors should always be chanted.
Thus ends the Śrī Sītā-kavaca within the Manohara-kāṇḍa of the glorious Ānanda-rāmāyaṇa by Vālmīki, which is part of the illustrious Śatakoṭi-rāmāyaṇa.
